passos.texto: Nanotechnology in anti-aging cosmetics: what 38 studies show, and what they don't show yet.
passos.extra: Systematic review by Alves, Nieri, Moreli, Constantino, Souza, Oshima-Franco and Grotto · Molecules, 2024

link.rotulo: Prefer to read it as text? Open the study page →

passos.texto: Look closely at the skin of the face. Wrinkles, loss of elasticity and dark spots are among the most common signs of aging.
The industry uses the term cosmeceuticals for products that claim a real effect on the skin. Many carry their active ingredients inside particles measured in nanometers: millionths of a millimeter.
The question of this review: what does research published from 2018 to 2023 show about these new ways of delivering anti-aging ingredients to the skin?
passos.fonte: Objective, at the end of the Introduction

visual.alt: Cross-section diagram of the skin: epidermis on top and, below, collagen and elastin fibers.

rotulos.texto: Sun and pollution generate reactive oxygen species (free radicals)
In menopause, hormonal changes worsen the loss of elasticity

cenas.alt: Diagram: sun and pollution generate free radicals in the skin, collagen breaks down and a wrinkle forms.

passos.texto: In the dermis, just below the surface, two proteins give the skin firmness and elasticity: collagen and elastin.
Sun and pollution generate reactive oxygen species, the free radicals. They break down collagen and impair its production.
With less collagen and elastin, the skin becomes more prone to wrinkles, sagging and loss of a youthful look.
Hormonal changes, especially during menopause, worsen the loss of elasticity.
passos.nota: According to the article, no topical treatment completely halts sun-induced aging; retinoids, antioxidants and sunscreens can reduce and delay the signs.

faixas.rotulo: Liposomes: from 20 nm to a few hundred µm

visual.legenda: Each mark is 10 times larger than the previous one. Dashed end: the article gives no maximum size for liposomes.

cenas.alt: Size ruler on a logarithmic scale: nanoparticles from 1 to 100 nm, nanoemulsions from 50 to 200 nm, liposomes from 20 nm to a few hundred micrometers; European definition of 1 to 100 nm and FDA criterion up to 1,000 nm.

passos.texto: According to the article, how well a cosmetic works depends not only on the active ingredient, but also on the technology that carries it to the right place in the skin and keeps it there long enough.
Nanoparticles measure 1 to 100 nanometers. Because they are so small, they have physical, chemical and biological properties that differ from the same material at ordinary size.
Nanoemulsions have droplets of 50 to 200 nm. Liposomes range from 20 nm to a few hundred micrometers.

There is no worldwide consensus on what counts as a nanomaterial in cosmetics. The European Union uses the range of 1 to 100 nm; the US FDA has no official definition, but in 2014 it began considering materials up to 1,000 nm.

itens.tam: gold, silver, zinc oxide, titanium dioxide

cenas.alt: Five schematic drawings: liposome, niosome, solid lipid nanoparticle, nanoemulsion and metallic nanoparticle.

passos.texto: These are the main delivery systems found in the review. Each one carries and releases the active ingredient in its own way.

Liposomes are tiny bubbles with a double layer of phospholipids around a water compartment; they carry ingredients that dissolve in water or in oil. Niosomes are similar but made of non-ionic surfactants: cheaper, more stable and easier to store.
Solid lipid nanoparticles have a solid fat core. Nanoemulsions are droplets of oil in water (or the reverse), well suited to carrying ingredients that dissolve in oil.
Among metallic nanoparticles, gold and silver ones act against bacteria and fungi; zinc oxide and titanium dioxide ones work as UV filters.

visual.inicio: papers found in PubMed and the grey literature
visual.alt: Selection funnel: 265 papers found; 135 excluded by title; 2 without free full text; 38 excluded by abstract; 52 excluded on full reading; 38 included.

cortes.rotulo: by title: reviews or injectable/subcutaneous use
on full reading: not focused on anti-aging

passos.texto: On August 24, 2023, the team searched PubMed and the grey literature for original papers in English, published from 2018 to 2023, using terms from the MeSH medical vocabulary.
passos.fonte: Materials and Methods; Figure 2 of the article

passos.texto: First filter, the title: 135 papers were removed because they were reviews or dealt with injectable or subcutaneous use.
Another 2 were not freely available in full.
Then the abstracts: 38 were off topic. The remaining 90 were read in full.
On full reading, 52 did not focus on anti-aging solutions. 38 papers remained.
passos.nota: Five reviewers took part in every step, and the papers were randomly redistributed among them at each phase.

niveis.sub: in vitro and ex vivo · Table 1

visual.nota: 17 + 11 + 10 = 38, from the rows of Tables 1 to 3. The article's text mentions 10 animal studies; Table 2 lists 11.

cenas.alt: Three rows of dots: 17 studies in cells and tissues, 11 in animals and 10 in people.

passos.texto: The 38 studies were grouped by type of test.
17 were done in cells or tissues outside the body (in vitro and ex vivo). Most used nanoparticles, followed by niosomes and liposomes.
11 were done in animals, mostly rats and mice, with the formulation applied to the skin.
10 were done in people, the final testing phase. Five used nanoparticles, two used microparticles and three did not report particle size.
passos.nota: All studies in people reported anti-aging action; the most frequent results were fewer wrinkles and more skin hydration.

visual.titulo: Studies that used each type of vehicle
visual.alt: Bars: liposomes in 7 studies, metallic nanoparticles in 4, niosomes in 3, nanoemulsions in 3, emulgel in 2, micelles in 2, microemulgel in 2 and 19 other types in 1 study each.
visual.eixo: Purple: lipid-based systems · yellow: metallic · gray: additional systems · the last bar groups 19 types from various families, each used in 1 study. A single study may have used more than one vehicle (one tested four). Data from Table 4.

passos.texto: Table 4 of the article lists 26 types of vehicle. The most frequent was the liposome, used in 7 studies.
Lipid-based systems, such as liposomes, niosomes and nanoemulsions, make up the largest group.
Next come metallic nanoparticles, in 4 studies.
For the authors, this shows a clear trend: nanotechnology is becoming a central tool both in research and in the development of new cosmetics.

visual.alt: Diagram of the skin with free radicals; then antioxidants neutralize some of them.

rotulos.texto: Inhibition of enzymes involved in aging

cenas.alt: Diagram: free radicals in the skin and antioxidants that neutralize them.

passos.texto: The ingredients tested were very varied and almost all of natural origin: gallic acid, lycopene, resveratrol, curcumin, bakuchiol, vitamin C, royal jelly and plant extracts, among others.
Most formulations showed antioxidant action: neutralizing free radicals, which the article identifies as an important mechanism of skin aging.
Some studies also showed reduced melanin, the pigment that forms dark spots when in excess.
Others showed inhibition of enzymes involved in skin aging and prevention of the changes in cell shape typical of aging.

itens.texto: improvement in wrinkles with an adenosine delivery system, compared with plain adenosine (0.04%).
itens.cuidado: Ref. 53: the exact number of participants was not reported (more than 20 women, over 19 years old), and the study's conclusion is general.

itens.texto: reduction in skin-surface melanin with niacinamide and sulforaphane in gold-decorated zeolite nanocomposites, compared with the plain versions (2% and 0.01%).
itens.cuidado: Same study (ref. 53), with the same limitations. Percentages as reported by the original authors.

itens.texto: Aspasomes with a vitamin C derivative treated melasma better than a conventional chemical peel, with no side effects.
itens.cuidado: Ref. 50: 20 Egyptian women aged 25 to 60; single-blind, single-center study.

cenas.alt: Three results from studies in people, each shown with its limitations.

passos.texto: Some studies in people reported large effects. But each number needs to be read together with the size and design of the study that produced it.
The same study reported reduced melanin, the pigment linked to dark spots.
Another study tested a vitamin C derivative in aspasomes, a type of vesicle, in women with melasma.

visual.alt: Diagram of a cell surrounded by small and large zinc oxide particles.

rotulos.texto: Accelerated aging in the cells (β-galactosidase test)
Both sizes: NF-kB and p53 ↑ · Nanog ↓

cenas.alt: Diagram: smaller zinc oxide particles accelerate signs of aging in cells.

passos.texto: Not every result was positive. In a study with zinc oxide nanoparticles (ref. 47), particle size made a difference.
Cells treated with the smaller particles showed an accelerated aging process.
Both sizes increased the activity of aging-related genes (NF-kB and p53) and decreased that of an anti-aging gene (Nanog).
passos.nota: The review notes that the study showed size-dependent toxicity but did not investigate the mechanisms behind it.

linhas.a: Can carry the ingredient deeper into the skin, with controlled and targeted release.
linhas.b: May face absorption limits, with effects concentrated in the surface layers.

linhas.a: Protects ingredients that degrade with air and light and extends shelf life.
linhas.b: Ingredients such as retinoic acid are highly unstable in air and light.

linhas.a: Sustained; may reduce the need to reapply.
linhas.b: More immediate and superficial; concentration peaks raise the risk of irritation.

linhas.a: Concern about particles crossing body barriers and reaching the bloodstream.
linhas.b: Long-term safety well documented, but retinoids can irritate and peel the skin.

cenas.alt: Table comparing nanotechnology and conventional products on five aspects.

passos.texto: In the Discussion, the authors compared nanotechnology products with conventional ones.
In favor of nanotechnology: it can carry the ingredient deeper and protect unstable ingredients.
But the sustained release of nanoparticles raises concern: they could cross biological barriers and enter the bloodstream. The safety of conventional products, by contrast, is well known.
For the authors, nanotechnology brings advances in efficacy, precise release and safety at lower doses, but concerns remain about long-term impact and higher cost.
passos.nota: They also see continuity: ingredients such as gallic acid, resveratrol, curcumin, propolis, niacinamide and adenosine appear both in lab tests and in tests in living organisms.

visual.titulo: How long each formulation's stability was tested
visual.alt: Columns showing how long each study tested stability: from 7 days to 10 months; 13 of the 38 studies without this information.

passos.texto: A cosmetic needs to keep its properties for months in storage. The article's limitation tables show how long each formulation's stability was tested.
In 13 of the 38 studies, this information was not reported, or the test was not done.
Among those that reported it, tests lasted from 7 days to 10 months. None went beyond a year, and the review points to the lack of long-term data as a recurring problem.
passos.fonte: Tables 5 to 7; Results, paragraph on Table 5

itens.texto: more than 20 women · exact number not reported
not stated · adequate, according to the review
about 20 to 25 per type of mask

visual.nota: Numbers from Table 7. “Ref.” follows the numbering of the article's references.

cenas.alt: Dots representing the participants of each study with people: 40, 14, 20, 6, 12, number not reported, 10, not stated, about 20 to 25 per mask and 13.

passos.texto: In the 10 studies with people, groups were small: from 6 to 40 participants, when the number was reported.
One study tested only 6 volunteers with normal skin. Others were limited to narrow age ranges, such as 25 to 40, which may not represent older people, precisely the audience for anti-aging products.
Three formulations contained parabens, ingredients the article considers potentially harmful. Three studies were single-blind and three were done at a single center.
Only one of the 10 (ref. 55) had no major limitations, according to the review: double-blind, with an adequate number of volunteers and an appropriate age range.

itens.texto: Long-term data are missing: several tests lasted hours, days or a few weeks.

itens.titulo: Whether nanoparticles are safe in the long term
itens.texto: There is concern about particles crossing body barriers, and long-term toxicology studies are lacking.
Several studies did not investigate the ingredients' mechanism of action.

itens.titulo: Whether animal results apply to aging people
itens.texto: In several studies, the animals' age was not reported or was not suitable for studying aging.
There is no worldwide consensus on what counts as a nanomaterial in cosmetics; each country adopts its own definition.

itens.titulo: Information the article does not provide
itens.texto: The review does not describe using a standardized tool to assess the quality of the included studies. The search was limited to PubMed and the grey literature, in English.

cenas.alt: List of questions still open about cosmetics with nanotechnology.

passos.texto: The review itself points out the gaps in the studies it analyzed.
passos.fonte: Results, paragraphs on Tables 5 to 7; Discussion

passos.texto: Answers are missing about mechanisms and about how the animal tests were designed.
And there are questions beyond the studies: regulation and the review's own method.
passos.ausente: use of a standardized tool to assess the quality of the included studies.

cenas.alt: Illustration: the view pulls back from nanoscale particles to the skin surface.

passos.texto: The 38 studies show why nanotechnology dominates anti-aging research: it can protect unstable ingredients, carry them deeper into the skin and release them gradually.
But the question that decides what reaches your skin, whether it works for years and safely, still awaits larger, longer studies with people of different ages.
Next time a label promises nanotechnology, it's worth asking: tested on whom, on how many people, and for how long?

creditos.como: Script, text and visualizations by GenoEvidence, based on the full text and the seven tables of the article (open-access version on Europe PMC, PMC11510423). All charts were redrawn from the published numbers; the original figures were not reproduced. No data were created. Where the article's text and tables give different numbers, this is noted in the scene. The drawings of skin, particles and cells are illustrative. References such as “ref. 47” and “ref. 53” follow the article's numbering.
